coherence.reasons: X is a tight four-part pyramid (demand, packaging, margin, timing and gates), and each summary claim maps to slides that carry it. Its one wobble is the fallback: it says AI must sit inside a plan and that mobile-first wins at low uptake, yet Gate 1 falls back to the $149 add-on in Q2. Y is also well ordered (why launch, package and price, trade-offs), but its governing thought and slide 9 title say Pro is the 'only option' meeting both NRR and margin. Y's own table contradicts that: the add-on stays above 76% margin and its NRR range (2.1–4.3) straddles the target just as Pro's (3.0–5.0) does. Y's sequencing slide also concedes mobile-first may lose less ARR, then rests on a timing claim that is asserted more than shown. X's headline claims match its evidence slightly more exactly.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer: launch inside a Pro tier with a usage allowance, sized off the paywall test, with mobile next. Y weighs a wider set of alternatives (don't launch, free in Core, add-on, Pro) against explicit criteria. It admits the sequencing is a close call on permanent ARR and separates deferred Pro revenue from permanently churned ARR. It also adds concrete mitigations for the mobile delay: Customer Success outreach, a dated roadmap, and no follow-on AI ahead of mobile. X's strength is sharp, actionable gates: the 2x conversion rule, the 25% uptake flip point, and the Q4 win-rate check that separates Routewise's discount from its AI. But X's sequencing comparison treats delayed Pro expansion as equivalent to churned ARR. Its add-on fallback also sits awkwardly with its own finding that low uptake favours mobile-first. Y's Q1 go/no-go does not say what happens on a no-go. On balance Y weighs the trade-offs slightly more completely.

evidence.reasons: Both get the four required calculations right: $8.06M vs $2.45M, inference of $32/$61/$130 per account, about $0.64M from the win-rate drop, and $2.89M for Pro. Both also flag survey bias, beta selection bias, the Routewise discount, and the flaw in the Sales memo. I checked X's margin and break-even figures (5,300 requests, 76.9%, a $0.09M loss without the allowance, 24.9% flip point) and they hold. Y uses the evidence more fully. It catches two internal inconsistencies in the pack: the top decile's 58% share against the 40% implied by Table 2, and 1,190 churned accounts against 1,372 implied. It notes that 56% of Routewise deals were already being lost before AI, links the flat fee to price-driven churn (22%) and its regressive effect on small accounts, and discounts the paywall rate below 14%. Y's weak points are the arbitrary 6.2/8.1 scaling to 10.7% (disclosed as an assumption), the 'only option' overclaim, and the asserted 'late 2028 at best' timing. X's weak point is equating deferred expansion with churn in its NRR-forgone chart, and it uses 14% as its add-on base despite calling it a ceiling.

revision.reasons: Both revise as the key expects: keep the launch, reject the $8M survey sizing, and move from the $149 add-on to a capped Pro tier. Y does this explicitly. It breaks the CPO's hypothesis into five conditions, gives each a verdict against the evidence, and states which parts survive (launch) and which fail (demand sizing, flat pricing). It also resets the plan figure to $1.7–2.9M. X reaches the same revision through its waterfall from $8M to $0.8M of gross profit and keeps the add-on only as a tested fallback. That is sound but less systematic about which parts of the hypothesis hold and why.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, numerically sound documents that avoid every trap in the key and land on the preferred recommendation. X is tighter, and its quantified gates and flip points are very usable in the room. Y gives the decision maker more: a fuller option comparison including free-in-Core, an honest treatment of the mobile trade-off with mitigations, catches of inconsistencies in the pack's own data, a range-based plan figure, and an explicit test of the CPO's hypothesis. Y's 'only option' overstatement and its somewhat asserted timing argument keep the margin small.
